From name to IP: the hostfile

To access a server it is more convenient to use a name than a 32-bit address: we type www.google.com, not its IP.

Every device has a hostfile: a text file with the static association between a name and an IP.

Originally Stanford maintained that file, and every machine downloaded it via FTP to learn the names with their IPs.

The limitation: it is a flat space, there cannot be two identical names.
A single text file for the whole network does not scale: another scheme was needed.
If someone else wanted to be called VERDE, they could not: names cannot be repeated.

The DNS (Domain Name System, RFC 1034 and 1035) replaces the file with a client-server scheme over a distributed database:

  • Resolver: the client. It sends the resolution request on behalf of the application.
  • Name server: receives the request and resolves the name to an IP address.

The resolver has a name server configured. The list of DNS servers is given by the DHCP server (the provider offers them) and can be seen with ipconfig.
The client does not know how to resolve names: it knows whom to ask.

The space is no longer flat. At the top is the root, represented by a dot. Below it, the top-level domains: .com, .edu, .org, and each country's code (.ar).

Each level delegates control: the root servers have a referral to those of .ar, which delegate to second-level domains (utn.edu.ar), which in turn have subdomains (frba, fra). Each entity is responsible for its domain.

A host's full name is its FQDN: host.subdomain.domain.tld.
With the trailing dot the name is complete: it is read from right to left, starting at the root.

FQDN (Fully Qualified Domain Name):
sistemas.frba.utn.edu.ar.
host · subdomain · domain · TLD · root
Zones of authority and server roles

A zone of authority is the portion of a domain a server is responsible for. That server has the zone file, with the domain's resource records, and the level above knows how to reach it. One server can maintain many zones.

  • Primary: stores the zone files locally.
  • Secondary: obtains the zone from a master (which can be a primary or a secondary).
  • Caching-only: has no zones; it only stores query results.
Primary and secondary replicate the zone for higher availability.
The DNS servers provided by the ISP are usually caching-only: they answer client queries, they do not host zones.

The resolver asks its preconfigured server. That query is recursive: it asks for a final answer. Either the IP address comes back, or an error message does.

If the server already knows the answer, it replies and queries no one. For an unknown FQDN it has to go out and look for it.

The request travels over UDP to port 53, which is lighter than TCP. If the response exceeds the maximum size and arrives truncated, the query is repeated using TCP.
Recursive = the client delegates the whole search: it wants the IP or an error, nothing in between.
The DNS server listens on port 53, both in UDP and TCP. UDP is tried first; if the response arrives truncated, it asks again over TCP.

The local DNS does not know frba.utn.edu.ar, so it asks around. Its queries are iterative: the other server can give the final answer or a hint about where to keep asking.

  • The root does not know the IP, but it knows who answers for .ar.
  • The .ar server has a referral to the name servers of utn.
  • That server has the zone: it gives the authoritative answer.

Only then does the local DNS reply to the client.
A single recursive query from the client triggers several iterative ones from the server.
Cache and TTL: don't ask twice

DNS servers cache the results of iterative queries so they do not repeat the whole process.

Each entry has a time to live (TTL), which is a configuration parameter of the zone: along with the IP, the zone's server states for how long the association is valid. When it expires, the entry is deleted.

When answering a recursive query, the remaining TTL is sent, so the client can also keep it in its cache and not ask again.
The zone's owner decides how long others may remember its answer.
The answer comes from the cache, not from the zone's server: that is why nslookup marks it as a non-authoritative answer.
Resource records: A, AAAA, MX, and CNAME

The zone file is made of resource records. When querying, you indicate which type of record you are looking for:

  • A: the most common. It associates a host name with an IP address. AAAA is the equivalent for IPv6.
  • MX (Mail Exchange): resolves the domain of an email address to the list of mail servers where it should be delivered.
  • CNAME (Canonical Name): an alias. It links one name to another name.
Each record type is handled differently: not everything in DNS is name → IP.
An email from Gmail to alguien@hotmail.com: Gmail's server asks the DNS for the MX records of hotmail.com and receives the list of mail servers to connect to in order to deliver it.

• nslookup gives access to the resolver: it lets you query the name server directly, choose which one to use (for example 8.8.8.8, Google's), and search by record type.
  • The local hostfile still exists and takes precedence: it is searched first and only then does it go to the DNS.
  • If it is unclear whether the name is complete, the system appends suffixes. With a trailing dot, the name is complete.
  • Reverse query: you give an IP and ask for the name. This is how traceroute names each router.
Search order: first the machine's hostfile, then the DNS server.
On Windows the hostfile is at System32\drivers\etc\hosts. What appears there wins over what the DNS says.

• From the flat hostfile to a distributed, hierarchical database: root, TLD, domains, subdomains.
  • Resolver (client) and name server; each zone has its responsible server.
  • Recursive query from the client; iterative ones from the server until the authoritative answer.
  • Cache with TTL to avoid repeating the process.
  • Port 53, UDP (TCP if truncated). A, AAAA, MX, and CNAME records.

What type of query does the resolver send to its configured DNS server?
Iterative: it accepts a referral to another server
Recursive: it expects the final answer, an IP or an error
Reverse: it sends an IP and expects a name
Authoritative: it only queries the zone's owner
The client makes a recursive query: it asks the server to give it the final answer, either the IP address or an error message.
The local DNS does not have frba.utn.edu.ar cached. Whom does it ask first?
It starts with the root, which does not know the IP but gives it the referral to the .ar servers; from there it keeps going down until the authoritative answer.
What protocol and port does a DNS query normally use?
UDP, port 53; TCP if the response arrives truncated
The server listens on port 53 for both UDP and TCP. The request is made over UDP because it is lighter; if the response exceeds the maximum size it is repeated over TCP.
What is an MX record for?
To associate a name with an IPv6 address
To create an alias for another name
To know which mail servers receive a domain's email
MX (Mail Exchange) resolves the domain of an email address to the list of mail servers to connect to in order to deliver it.
